result.summary: The terrified Chorus of Theban women rush in, praying loudly to the gods as the Argive host approaches. Eteocles returns and angrily scolds them for spreading panic, and orders them to be silent, stay indoors and pray for victory. He makes a vow to the gods and goes to post six defenders at the gates, himself the seventh.

scenes.title: The Chorus prays in terror
scenes.summary: The women of Thebes hear the enemy approach and cry out to Ares, Zeus, Pallas, Poseidon, Cypris, Apollo, Hera and Artemis to save the city.
scenes.stakes: The women fear capture of Thebes and their own enslavement.

scenes.title: Eteocles rebukes the women
scenes.summary: Eteocles scolds the Chorus for spreading cowardice, trades sharp lines with them, and silences them. He gives a vow to the gods and leaves to post the seven champions at the gates.
scenes.stakes: Eteocles risks the city falling through panic from within, and his own authority.

analysis.text: The scene contrasts the women's emotional religious panic with Eteocles' stern, rational command, showing the strain of civic duty under siege.
Eteocles' remarks reflect Athenian assumptions that war and politics are male affairs, while women's public ritual and lament could be seen as dangerous.

fun_facts.text: The Chorus's entry describes sounds of the attack rather than showing it, since Greek tragedy could not stage battles.

language_notes.text: "In the van" means at the front; the horsemen lead the advancing army.
A harbinger is a forerunner that announces what is coming; here the dust warns of the army.
Sacred robes and coronals (garlands) were draped on divine images as offerings when asking a god for help.
A casque is a helmet; erstwhile means formerly.
The fortress of Cadmus is Thebes, founded by Cadmus; the Argives are the besieging army from Argos.
The weapon that spears fish is Poseidon's trident; he was also god of horses.
Cypris is Aphrodite; she was mother of Harmonia, wife of Cadmus, so Thebans claim descent from her.
Lord of the Wolf is Apollo Lykeios; the chorus plays on the wolf title, asking him to act as a wolf against the enemy.
Onca was a Theban title of Athena, linked to a sanctuary at Thebes, here guarding the seven gates.
"Insufferable" means unbearable; "ye" is the archaic plural "you". The "images of the gods" are the statues of the city's protecting deities.
"Whatsoever is betwixt" means anyone neither clearly man nor woman; Eteocles is stressing that no one is exempt from his authority.
"Pipes" here are the axle-boxes of the chariot wheels, which screech as the wheels turn; the translator marks this with a footnote.
Ancient belief held that gods abandoned a city when it fell, so Eteocles uses the idea to turn the women's prayer toward holding the walls.
"Saw" means a proverbial saying. Obedience, Success and Preserver (Saviour) are personified in this maxim.
Ares is the god of war; calling blood his "food" means war feeds on human death, so lamenting it is pointless.
"Adread" is an archaic form of "afraid"; "ports" here means the city gates, not harbours.
"Plague on thee" is a curse meaning roughly "Curse you!", expressing Eteocles' angry impatience.
"Boon" is a favour; "trifling" means small. Eteocles asks for a small favour, which is silence.
"Anon" means soon; the Chorus says it will understand what he wants shortly.
"Likes me better" means "pleases me more"; "likes" is used impersonally in the older English way.
"Wont" means custom; "jubilance" is joyous shouting. The women are told to raise the ritual cry that accompanied sacrifice.
Dirce's springs and Ismenus' stream are the waters of Thebes, local sacred places whose guardian powers Eteocles invokes.
"Outlets" are the city's gates; "tenour" in the previous line meant general purport.

context_notes.text: Ares, god of war, was closely tied to Thebes: Cadmus's dragon was his, and Harmonia was his daughter.
Pallas is Athena, born from the head of Zeus and goddess of war strategy and cities.
Artemis, maiden goddess of the hunt and archery, was daughter of Leto and sister of Apollo.
Stoning by the community was a traditional ancient punishment for serious offences against the city.
The Chorus are Theban women; they address Eteocles as son of Oedipus, the former king, and are terrified by the sounds of the approaching Argive army.
The Chorus are Theban women who hear the besieging Argive army approaching and cling to the statues of the gods in terror.
Zeus, king of the gods, wielded the thunderbolt; the women beg him to strike the attackers with it.
Vows to the gods promised sacrifice and dedicated spoils if the city was saved, a standard Greek way of seeking divine help.
Seven attackers face seven gates; Eteocles will defend the seventh himself, a choice that has fateful consequences later in the play.

literary_notes.text: The hoofbeats are compared to a resistless torrent lashing a mountainside, conveying the overwhelming force of the cavalry.
The repeated "who then" shows the women's helplessness and pushes them toward prayer.
The army becomes a seething human wave of crests driven by the winds of Ares, making war a storm.
Apollo's wolf title is turned into a command to act as a wolf, tying cult name to hoped-for action.
The air going mad with flying spears exaggerates the chorus's terror and the din of battle.
Eteocles' open hostility to women shows him as stern, authoritarian and dismissive, a commander who treats fear as a female weakness.
The ship in a tossing sea stands for the city under threat; running from stern to prow is useless, like the women's panic.
His curt, sarcastic reply mocks the Chorus's warning and ironically asks for willful deafness, though the approaching danger is real.
Eteocles, the commander, claims the women's panic enslaves him and the city, reversing the Chorus's fear of slavery.
He turns from the women to address Zeus directly, voicing his exasperation and misogyny.
Fear is imagined as running away with her tongue, as if her speech were a horse out of control.
Eteocles placing himself as the seventh defender hints at the coming confrontation with his brother at the seventh gate.
